items.article: A Massachusetts judge has denied Lindsay Clancy's attempt to have the murder charges against her thrown out , clearing the way for prosecutors to pursue a retrial in the high-profile case involving the deaths of her three children. In a ruling issued Thursday, Plymouth Superior Court Judge William F. Sullivan rejected the defense's Rule 25 motion for a required finding of not guilty following September's mistrial. Under Massachusetts law, a Rule 25 motion asks a judge to determine whether prosecutors presented sufficient evidence for a reasonable jury to convict. Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, argued the Commonwealth failed to prove two key elements of its case: that Clancy killed her three children and that she was criminally responsible for her actions at the time. Sullivan disagreed, finding that prosecutors presented enough evidence for a reasonable jury to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy committed the killings and could be held criminally responsible. “There was evidence introduced, both physical and circumstantial, that would permit a rational trier of fact to find beyond a reasonable doubt the elements of the charge of murder," Sullivan wrote. The decision does not determine guilt or innocence. Rather, it means the judge found the evidence presented during the first trial was legally sufficient for the case to proceed to a new jury.

items.article: “Some have called Alzheimer’s ‘diabetes of the brain’ or ‘type 3 diabetes.’” Though it doesn’t currently have a cure – or even a single diagnostic test – some researchers are beginning to see dementia as potentially “treatable” . A recent report from Alzheimer’s Disease International (ADI) and health writer Paul Gallagher showed that experts have become “optimistic” about the disease due to newly released drugs and an “unprecedented” boom in dementia research. An older addition to that corpus is a 2020 paper that suggests that dementia could be considered a third kind of diabetes. It says that the relationship between poorly-controlled blood sugar and dementia onset is “so strong that some have called Alzheimer’s ‘diabetes of the brain’ or ‘type 3 diabetes (T3D)’”. Alzheimer’s Society shared that people with type 2 diabetes (when the body becomes more resistant to the sugar-regulating hormone, insulin) are more likely to develop dementia than the general population. The same is also true of those with type 1 diabetes, which is an autoimmune condition where the body attacks its own insulin-making cells.
